capital: Mbabane (administrative capital) / Lobamba (royal and legislative capital)
summary: A landlocked monarchy in southern Africa, renamed from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018; it is one of the few countries in the world where the king still holds real power.

ranking.name: Zionist and other African independent churches
ranking.description: In the early 20th century the Zionist movement, originating in Zion City, Illinois, in the United States, spread to South Africa and was then brought home by Eswatini people working in South African mines, developing into African independent churches that stress Holy Spirit healing, prophets and white-robe rituals. These churches allow traditional customs such as ancestor veneration and polygamy to be kept and are closer to local culture than Western missions; King Sobhuza II also expressed support for them, and so they became the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1844 King Mswati II received a visit from Wesleyan missionaries, and Protestant missions began from then; the Anglican, Lutheran and Nazarene churches and others later set up churches as well. The missions ran schools and hospitals and trained many of the elite of the colonial period and after independence, so Protestantism has a deep influence among better-educated city dwellers.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in the early 20th century by missionaries of Italian religious orders, who then established a diocese in Manzini and ran a large number of schools, hospitals and social service institutions. Because the quality of education in Catholic schools is good, many families send their children there and the number of believers has grown accordingly, making it the third-largest religious group.

ranking.name: Other (traditional beliefs, Baháʼí Faith, etc.)
ranking.description: Eswatini traditional belief centers on ancestral spirits, holding that ancestors protect their descendants, while the king is a sacred figure linking the people with the ancestral spirits. The annual Incwala royal ceremony and the Umhlanga (Reed Dance) are still important national rituals, and many Christians take part as usual. The Baháʼí Faith arrived in the mid-20th century and has few followers.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived mainly with South Asian traders and with immigrants from Mozambique, Malawi and elsewhere, and in the late 20th century mosques and communities were established in the cities. Because the Eswatini state and royal culture are deeply influenced by Christianity and traditional belief, Muslims have always been only a very small minority.

religion.background: The Swazi traditionally believe in ancestral spirits, and the king plays the role of religious leader in the royal ceremonies. Wesleyan missionaries came to Swaziland in 1844, and Christian denominations then set up churches and schools one after another; during the British protectorate of 1903–1968, mission education became more widespread. In the early 20th century the Zionist movement arrived from South Africa and merged with traditional belief to form African independent churches, which became the largest religious group. Today most people are Christian, but the royal ceremonies and belief in ancestral spirits still deeply influence social life.

language.official: The official languages are Swazi (siSwati) and English.

ranking.name: Swazi (siSwati)
ranking.description: Swazi belongs to the Nguni branch of the Bantu languages and is quite close to Zulu. In the early 19th century Kings Sobhuza I and Mswati II united the various clans and founded the kingdom; the country's name "Swazi" derives from Mswati II, and Swazi became the national common language. Because Eswatini is one of the few single-nation states in Africa, almost all citizens have Swazi as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Zulu
ranking.description: Zulu is the main language of neighboring South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal Province and is highly mutually intelligible with Swazi. Early missionaries taught in Swaziland using Zulu Bibles and teaching materials, and only in the late 20th century did the written form of Swazi replace Zulu in schools, so Zulu is still used in the border areas and in some families.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: The status of English comes from the British protectorate of 1903–1968, when English was used in administration, law and education from secondary school up. After independence in 1968 English became an official language alongside Swazi, in common use in government, business and higher education, though very few people have English as a mother tongue.

language.history: Swazi belongs to the Nguni branch and became the common language after the founding of the Swazi kingdom in the 19th century. Early missionaries mostly used Zulu for preaching and education, and a written form of Swazi developed later. From 1903 British protectorate rule made English the language of administration and education. After independence in 1968 Swazi and English were both official languages, and in the late 20th century Swazi formally entered school education, becoming an important symbol of national identity.

ranking.name: Pap (maize porridge)
ranking.description: A thick maize porridge made by stirring white maize meal into boiling water, with a firm texture, which is shaped by hand into small balls and dipped in stew, vegetables or sour milk.
ranking.history: Maize is native to the Americas and was brought to southeastern Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries, gradually replacing traditional sorghum and millet because of its high yield. In the 19th–20th centuries many Eswatini men worked in South African mines, where maize porridge was the workers' ration food, which made it the staple of all of southern Africa. Today almost every Eswatini household eats maize porridge every day, and it is the most basic daily food.
ranking.imageCredit: Paresh Jai from Nairobi, Kenya・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Emasi (sour milk)
ranking.description: Fresh cow's milk is put in a gourd or container and left to ferment naturally into thick sour milk, with a slightly sour taste, often poured over maize porridge and eaten together.
ranking.history: The Nguni peoples have lived by raising cattle since ancient times, and cattle are not only a source of food but also a symbol of wealth and of bridewealth (called "lobola"), so dairy products have an important place in the diet. Traditionally milk is fermented in gourds, and sour milk keeps more easily than fresh milk, suiting rural life without refrigeration. It is a traditional food shared by the Swazi, the Zulu and the Xhosa and is still regarded as nutritious and a taste of home.

ranking.name: Chakalaka (spicy vegetable relish)
ranking.description: A spicy vegetable relish cooked from onion, tomato, bell pepper, carrot and baked beans with curry powder and chili, often served with maize porridge or grilled meat.
ranking.history: This relish is generally believed to have originated in the gold-mining districts and Black townships of Johannesburg, South Africa, in the 20th century, reportedly as a side dish cooked by miners from Mozambique from canned beans, tomatoes and chili, with the curry powder coming from the local Indian community. Because many Eswatini people also went to work in South African mines, the relish came to Eswatini with the migrant workers and became a common side dish at barbecues and family meals.
ranking.imageCredit: philipp from cape town, south africa・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Biltong (dried beef)
ranking.description: Beef cut into long strips, cured with salt and spices and hung to air-dry in a cool place, making a dried meat that keeps for a long time, salty and savory with a very chewy texture.
ranking.history: In the days before refrigerators, herders and hunters in southern Africa preserved meat by salting and air-drying, and the dry winter climate is especially suited to making dried meat. In Eswatini tradition, cattle are often slaughtered for weddings, royal ceremonies and important festivals, and the leftover meat is made into dried meat to be shared and kept. This practice is similar to South Africa's biltong, and it is still a common snack and food for guests.
ranking.imageCredit: Delia du Plessis・CC BY-SA 3.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Sorghum beer
ranking.description: A traditional beer fermented from sorghum or maize malt, low in alcohol, thick and slightly sour in taste, and cloudy milky white in color.
ranking.history: Sorghum beer is a traditional drink of the Nguni peoples of southern Africa, traditionally brewed by women; at weddings, initiation rites and ancestor ceremonies it is first offered to the ancestral spirits and then shared with everyone. It is also an indispensable drink at royal ceremonies such as the Incwala and at community work gatherings. Because it is rich in malt and grain, it was also regarded in the past as a source of nutrition, and it still plays an important role in rural festivals.
